title: Analysis: RBA's ugly outlook spells tough times
full_text:
The Reserve Bank of Australia's latest interest rate rise to an 18-year high of 4.85 per cent is accompanied by an ugly set of numbers in its 75-page quarterly Statement on Monetary Policy, which exposes how fragile the economy is.
RBA governor Michele Bullock admits "it is going to make people feel like it's a recession because they feel poorer", even though the bank is not forecasting a technical recession for the overall economy.
Bullock also undercut Treasurer Jim Chalmers' political spin, after he again blamed inflation and the fifth rate rise this year on the Middle East war pushing up fuel prices. But she was not indulging the treasurer on Tuesday. She stepped up to the podium at her press conference and straight off the bat said she wanted to be "very clear" that the bank was raising rates in response to domestic capacity pressures.
"So yes, we have a domestic home-grown inflation problem," she said.
That is, the AI-driven data centre boom, elevated federal and state government spending and shrinking productivity.
Worryingly, inflation is much worse than expected just three months ago.
House prices are falling faster than previously thought, with "tax changes amplifying the effects of monetary policy", the RBA says.
Bullock, armed with a new killer RBA chart comparing the housing market during monetary tightening cycles since 1990, attributed the sharp fall in investor home loans to Labor's May budget changes to capital gains tax and negative gearing.
Economic momentum is weakening. GDP growth is tipped to ease to 1.3 per cent by late next year, or virtually stagnant in per-person terms.
Real wages will be going backwards until at least late 2027.
Consumer spending is sluggish. Business profit margins are shrinking, as firms struggle to fully pass through higher costs for labour, energy and fuel.
That's why Bullock is warning it will feel like a recession to many people.
The unemployment rate is tipped to drift up to 5.1 per cent by late 2028 and the RBA's internal models estimate it needs to be around this new higher mark to subdue inflation.
By historical standards, the labour market is still holding up pretty well.
But the lift in the cash rate on Tuesday by 0.25 of a percentage point to 4.85 per cent may not be the last rise to tame inflation. Six RBA board members voted for the rate increase and three members opposed the higher borrowing costs, with Bullock suggesting they will now "take stock" for a while - probably until next year.
Yet, the RBA's analysis shows the so-called "neutral" rate of interest required to control inflation may be rising globally and in Australia.
"By itself, a rising neutral rate would imply that any given path for policy rates is somewhat less restrictive than previously assessed," the RBA notes.
Headline inflation has been significantly upgraded by almost 1 percentage point this year and is not expected to fall back below 3 per cent until late next year.
The RBA points to soaring international prices for fuel, chemicals and fertilisers due to the war in the Middle East and the artificial intelligence boom that is pushing up prices globally for data centres, iPhones and computer consoles.
But the sting in the tail for Chalmers is that the RBA is blaming home-grown factors for driving up the bank's much more closely watched and preferred measure of underlying inflation.
The central bank blames price pressures in labour-intensive and wage-sensitive market services, such as eating out, on award and minimum wage increases introduced by the Labor-backed Fair Work Commission.
"We assess that the upward surprise in underlying inflation reflects stronger-than-expected domestic capacity pressures this year," says the RBA. "This strength primarily reflected domestic capacity pressures and, to a lesser extent, pass-through of conflict-related cost pressures (such as from food and fuel inputs)."
In other words, shrinking productivity means the supply side of the economy is less able to absorb private and public spending pressures without spurring inflation. Labour productivity is tipped to shrink this year, before turning slightly positive next year.
The politically attuned bank is more muted on the contribution of federal and state government spending to inflation, only noting that the public infrastructure pipeline was stronger than expected.
Finally, this assessment assumes the RBA's latest forecasts are broadly accurate. Since the last statement in August, its forecasts have been blown out of the water and the bank has continually been caught out by higher inflation and households' resilience to interest rate rises.
The RBA has built more upside inflation risks into its forecasts, but potential renewed US strikes on Iran after the midterm election, the inflationary AI boom, pre-election spending by federal and state governments, and the housing downturn all pose additional risks.
Nine Entertainment Co.
